In 1859, the Sun fired a storm at Earth so powerful, that telegraph machines burst into flames.
And some operators kept sending messages, with their batteries unplugged.
On the first of September, astronomer Richard Carrington was sketching sunspots,
when a blinding white flash burst out of the Sun. By the time he found a witness, it was gone.
Seventeen hours later, the Sun's reply arrived.
The night sky turned blood red. Auroras glowed as far south as Cuba. And gold miners in the Rockies woke at midnight, and started cooking breakfast.
Then the telegraph networks went mad. Sparks leapt from the machines. Paper burst into flames.
In Boston and Portland, two operators switched off their batteries, and chatted for two hours, using only the aurora.
It is called the Carrington Event. The strongest solar storm in recorded history.
Today, a storm like that could cripple satellites and power grids.
Scientists say the next one is not a question of if, but when.
